author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
Design philosophy of my next gen meta-agent/meta-harness
(whatever you want to call it, to me, it is just a bunch of python scripts)

1. No vendor lock-in. No lab, cloud, agent harness, or storage service is required. Every integration has an alternative—agents via Herdr, web, or desktop; compute via local, SSH, or lab-hosted machines; mail via Dropbox or Box. Swapping vendors is a catalog entry (agents.json, .env), not a redesign.

2. LLMs are interchangeable. Choose models by the best cost-versus-intelligence trade-off for each task, not vendor loyalty. Routing uses measured quotas, usage, API-equivalent cost, and free-token offers; the Agent field names the harness, never a model family.

3. Committed GitHub code is the source of truth. Not chat history, agent memory, or local worktrees. Specs, prompts, data, and important decisions are committed; an agent that has not pushed its work has not done it.

4. Manage the build with GitHub issues and Projects. Work is decomposed into issues, dependencies use native blocked_by edges, execution follows Iterations, releases are milestones, and comments provide the evidence trail. github_project.md

5. Treat tokens and compute as budgets. Track subscription quota, API spend, and machine time—CPU, memory, and VMs—like any resource. dashboards.md machines.md A cheaper model can trade more attempts, tests, and review rounds for capability; the orchestrator makes that trade explicitly.

6. Know each agent's machine and capabilities. Every loop runs locally, on a remote host, or in a lab VM; a cloud agent is still just another computer with an OS, filesystem, network policy, and limits. Record each run's machine and capabilities—internet, package installs, web search, scraping, browser/desktop control, GPU, session lifetime—and dispatch work only where they exist. Never assume; verify. machines.md

7. Support both command-center and observer modes. As a command center, it launches and drives agents. As an observer, it tracks work a human starts in any AI app—e.g., “work on GitHub issue N”—through the project, repository, and usage data. Both modes must work; neither is required.

8. Build from first principles, not protocols. Agent protocols and plugin standards change. Communicate through universal interfaces—terminal, web page, desktop window—and coordinate through git, GitHub issues, and shared files. Protocols may help, but nothing may depend on them.

9. Optimize for batch, not real time. Dispatch and check agents every few hours, daily, or every few days. Prioritize throughput, cost, and correctness over latency; support large efforts that run for weeks, survive restarts, and resume where they left off.

10. The human directs; agents build; the repo teaches. The human guides agents to build the system without hand-writing code, then learns from committed code, specs, and issue history. Keep the repository self-explanatory: current specs, traceable issues, and recorded decisions
